# Exploring Data

## Overview

In these notes we will look at a few common methods for visualizing data. There are two main types of data we will be concerned with in this class: **categorical** and **quantatative** data. Categorical data is when the results are descriptive (not numerical) and can be organized into a finite number of answers. Examples of categorical data include: favorite color, blood type, methods of transportation, favorite food, etc. Quantative data is data that is numerical. This can include: weights, heights, times, exam scores, etc. 

The tools we use to visualize data depend on whether the data is catagorical or quantatative. 

## Bar and Pie Charts

**Bar** and **Pie charts** are two ways to visualize the distribution of **categorical** data. Suppose 250 individuals were polled about how they commute to work and the following results were obtained, 

| Category | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Car | 134 |
| Public Transit | 58 |
| Bike | 44 | 
| Walk | 24 |

We can visualize this data using either a bar or pie chart. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-vs-pie
#| fig-cap: "The same data shown as a bar chart (left) and a pie chart (right)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9

commute <- c(Car = 134, Transit = 58, Bike = 44, Walk = 24)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

barplot(commute, main = "Bar Chart", ylab = "Amount", ylim = c(0, 150))

pie(commute, main = "Pie Chart",
col = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "forestgreen", "firebrick"))
```

Creating a bar chart is simple, each **categorical variable** gets a bar where the height is represented by the number of respondents in the dataset. To create a pie chart, we start by computing the percentage of the whole for each category,

| Category | Count | Percentage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car | 134 | 53.6% |
| Public Transit | 58 | 23.2% |
| Bike | 44 | 17.6% |
| Walk | 24 | 9.6% |

The angle each pie slice gets corresponds to its percentage. For example, the *transit* category should have an interior angle that is 23.2% of 360 degrees, or 

$$0.232 \cdot 360 = 83.52 \text{ degrees.}$$

::: {#exm-pie}
A class of 32 students was surveyed about whether they prefer morning, afternoon, or evening classes. The results are given in the table below. 

| Time of Day | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Morning | 10 | 
| Afternoon | 14 |
| Evening | 8 |

To compute the percentage of votes of each category, we divide the quantity by the total number of students, 32.

| Time of Day | Count | Percentage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morning | 10 | 10/32 = 31.25% |
| Afternoon | 14 | 14/32 = 43.75% |
| Evening | 8 | 8/32 = 25% |

```{r}
#| label: class-time-pie
#| fig-cap: "A pie chart depicting student class time preferences."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6

class <- c(Morning = 10, Afternoon = 14, Evening = 8)

pie(class, main = "Pie Chart",
col = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "forestgreen"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Picking the Best Visual"}
In what ways are bar and pie charts similar and in what ways are they different? What are some benefits to a pie chart over a bar chart (and vice versa)?
:::

Don't worry so much about creating a pie or bar chart by hand as we will use technology in this class. The below example explain how to create the graphs using StatCrunch. 

::: {#exm-statcrunch}
## Basic Visuals in StatCrunch
A company has collected data on 500 customers. [Open this dataset in StatCrunch](https://www.statcrunch.com/app/index.html?dataid=5131375){target="_blank"}. Use StatCrunch to create a bar chart of customer satisfaction by doing the following:

1. Under Graph, select Bar Plot, then With Data.
2. In the pop up screen, select the column SatisfactionRating. Set Type to Frequency and then hit Compute!

Next create a pie chart of the customer regions by selecting Graph > Pie Chart > With Data. 
:::

## Histograms

Bar and pie charts are a great way to visualize *categorical* data. Now we want to address ways to visualize **quantitative** data, or data that is in the form of numbers. 

::: {#exm-quantdata}
## Quantitative Data
Some example of quantitative data include: test scores, age, height, weight, (systolic) blood pressure, etc. 
:::

A good way to look at quantitative data is to use a **histogram**. A histogram breaks the range of all possible values into smaller intervals, then counts how many observation fall into each window. This looks kind of like a bar chart, but the bars sit right next to each other. 

::: {#exm-testscores}
Students in a calculus class obtain the following scores on the midterm exam, 

$$100, 85, 91, 76, 88, 82, 95, 62, 84, 79, 90, 73, 87, 81, 92, 77, 86, 83, 80, 89, 74, 93, 85, 79, 82$$

The lowest score is a 62 and the highest score is 100. Let's break down the range $[60,100]$ into intervals of length 5.

| Interval | Count |
| --- | --- | 
| (60,65] | 1 |
| (65,70] | 0 |
| (70,75] | 2 |
| (75,80] | 5 |
| (80,85] | 7 |
| (85,90] | 5 |
| (90,95] | 4 |
| (95,100] | 1 |

From this we can make a histogram. 

```{r}
#| label: test-hist
#| fig-cap: "A histogram of test scores."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
scores <- c(100, 85, 91, 76, 88, 82, 95, 62, 84, 79, 90, 73, 87, 81, 92, 77, 86, 83, 80, 89, 74, 93, 85, 79, 82)

hist(scores,
     breaks = c(60, 65, 70, 75, 80, 85, 90, 95, 100),
     main = "Distribution of Exam Scores",
     xlab = "Score",
     ylab = "Frequency")
```
:::


It is typical to call the intervals of a histogram **bins**, although the reading on WAMAP will call them **classes**. A histogram should always have bins of the same length. It can be misleading to use different bin lengths in the same way it is misleading to use breaks on the vertical axis of bar charts. 

Most computer programs will set automatic bin sizes based on the distribution of the data you get it, although you will typically have an option to manually input bin specifications. In StatCrunch you are give the optional inputs of the starting value and the bin width. 

::: {.callout-important title="Bin Endpoints"}
For whatever computer program you use, make sure you know how the **endpoints** of your bin intervals are treated. In Example @exm-testscores, I wrote intervals like (70,75] which means 70 is excluded from the bin and 75 is included in the bin. The statistical programming language R (what generates the graphs in these notes) uses right inclusive bins, however StatCrunch uses *left* inclusive bins. 
:::

The histograms below represent *the same* data, just with different bin sizes. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist-bins
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of the same dataset with different bin widths."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9

set.seed(123)
zeros    <- rep(0, 100)
near0    <- runif(5, 0.1, 0.9)
mid1     <- runif(300, 1, 4)
data     <- c(zeros, near0, mid1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

hist(data,
     breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4),
     col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "Bin Width 1",
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Frequency")

hist(data,
     breaks = seq(0, 4, by = 0.1),
     col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "Bin Width 0.1",
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Frequency")
```

From the histogram on the left the data looks *uniform* across the values 0-4. When we choose a small bin width though, we see a different behavior emerge.

## High Tide Heights
The following histogram shows high tide heights over the month of July at a beach.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tidehist
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of high tide heights in July."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6

heights <- c(2.05, 2.06, 1.99, 1.89, 1.86, 1.74, 1.74, 1.74, 1.5, 1.4,
             1.4, 1.32, 1.23, 1.11, 1.15, 1.21, 1.06, 1.16, 1.1, 1.22,
             1.25, 1.47, 1.48, 1.7, 1.78, 1.84, 1.73, 1.94, 2.02, 2.06,
             1.93, 1.99, 1.91, 1.87, 1.95, 1.71, 1.69, 1.66, 1.45, 1.4,
             1.34, 1.26, 1.11, 1.17, 1.26, 1.03, 1.25, 1.23, 1.23, 1.52,
             1.5, 1.44, 1.64, 1.77, 1.8, 1.95, 1.95, 2.06, 2.15, 2.0,
             2.06, 1.98)

hist(heights,
     breaks = 8,
     main = "High Tide Heights",
     xlab = "Tide Height (m)", ylab = "Frequency")
```

The number of high tides that were more than 2 meters is given by the total in the last two bins, $6+1=7$. To compute the percentage of high tides that were more than two meters, note that the total number of high tides is $62$. 

$$ \frac{7}{62}\cdot 100 \approx 11.29\%$$
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Information Lost"}
What kinds of information do we lose by only seeing a histogram of the data? 
:::
